newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's industrial giants prepare to downsize.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's industrial giants prepare to downsize.

text.p: South Korea's top business conglomerates are set to announce a freeze on wages and moves to trim their bloated workforces to improve sagging profits, industry officials said on Monday.
Powerful unions reacted with outrage to the plan, which is in line with an austerity package unveiled last week by Finance Minister Han Seung-soo.

Chairmen of the top 30 business conglomerates, known as "chaebol," are expected to agree on September 17 to freeze total spending on salaries and benefits next year, an official with the Federation of Korean Industries said.
Under a plan jointly worked out by their planning offices, they will also endorse early retirement schemes.
South Korean labour laws make it virtually impossible to forcibly lay off workers.

"Our competitiveness is bumping against a ceiling of high costs and low efficiency," federation director Shim In said in an interview. "The situation will be serious unless we take significant action."
Welcoming the move, the Korea Federation of Small Business said on Monday that it would follow suit.
The chaebol dominates South Korea's economy and sets the standard for pay increases. Average pay has risen by 15 percent annually since 1987, and last year was up by 11.2 percent.
Wage rises have outpaced productivity, eroding the international competitiveness of South Korean products.

Profits announced by 415 listed manufacturing firms, including the most important chaebol units, slumped by 53.17 percent in the first half. Profits have also been hit by falling prices of key export items such as semiconductors and steel, and a weakening Japanese yen.
"We will risk labour strikes to protect our rights. Labour-management relations will be drawn into a whirlpool next year," said Choi Dae-yul, chief spokesman of the Federation of Korean Trade Unions.
A statement issued by the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions said that, "by mobilising all our efforts, we will fight until the decision is withdrawn."

A series of labour disputes this year over pay and conditions paralysed large parts of the auto industry. Worker unrest that threatened key public services was averted only by last-minute compromises.

"Many companies have come to the conclusion that persistently rising wages have burdened profits," said Lee Han-ku, president of Daewoo Economic Research Institute. "They stand at the crossroads of going bust or surviving."
Spending on wages accounts for 10 percent of average company sales, Federation of Korean Industries figures show.
High wages have driven chaebol overseas, leading to fears of a hollowing-out of local industry. "The wage freeze seems to be an alternative to prevent further hollowing-out," Lee said.

Labour-intensive textile concerns, struggling against competition from low-wage Asian countries, are expected to be the most aggressive. Sunkyong Industries, a polyester yarn maker, said it would cut 800 employees from its workforce of 3,600 by offering severance payments.
Steelmaker POSCO and Kolon Group have already decided to freeze wages for executives, spokesmen said.
Samsung Electronics, a unit of Samsung Group, plans to introduce early retirement and cut off non-strategic business lines, a spokeswoman said.
